claims.text: Initial investigations should include a full blood count, C-reactive protein, and blood cultures to assess for early-onset sepsis.
A lumbar puncture is recommended if meningitis is suspected, as it is a common complication of early-onset sepsis.
Preterm birth at 28 weeks with a history of prolonged rupture of membranes is a recognised risk factor for early-onset neonatal infection.
Serial monitoring of respiratory rate and CRP levels every 2–4 hours helps detect evolving sepsis in the first 72 hours.
Escalation to intensive care is warranted if the infant shows persistent tachypnoea (>45 breaths/min) or a rising CRP beyond 10 mg/L.
Parents should be informed that early-onset sepsis can present subtly and that close observation is essential in the first 72 hours.

packet.evaluation_question: Explain appropriate initial diagnostic investigations for suspected early-onset sepsis and the limitations of laboratory tests. Gestation 28 weeks; age 6 hours; setting hospital birth.

evidence.text: For babies with suspected late-onset neonatal infection or meningitis who have been admitted from home, treat according to recommendations 1.8.6 and 1.8.7 in NICE's guideline on suspected sepsis in under 16s. [2021]

For guidance on managing prelabour rupture of membranes at term, see NICE's guideline on intrapartum care. [2021] Box 1: Risk factors for early-onset neonatal infection, including 'red flags' Red flag risk factor: • suspected or confirmed infection in another baby in the case of a multiple pregnancy Other risk factors: • invasive group B streptococcal infection in a previous baby or maternal group B streptococcal colonisation, bacteriuria or infection in the current pregnancy • pre-term birth following spontaneous labour before 37 weeks' gestation • confirmed rupture of membranes for more than 18 hours before a pre-term birth • confirmed rupture of membranes for more than 24 hours before a term birth [2026] • suspected or confirmed maternal sepsis in the intrapartum or early postpartum period [2021, amended 2026] • suspected or confirmed chorioamnionitis [2021, amended 2026]

Risk factors and clinical indicators: early- onset neonatal infection 1.9 Identification and assessment before birth 1.9.1 For women, trans men and non-binary people in labour, identify and assess any risk factors for early-onset neonatal infection (see box 1 on risks factors for early- onset neonatal infection). Throughout labour, monitor for any new risk factors. [2021] 1.9.2 For guidance on managing prelabour rupture of membranes at term, see NICE's guideline on intrapartum care. [2021] Box 1: Risk factors for early-onset neonatal infection, including 'red flags' Red flag risk factor: • suspected or confirmed infection in another baby in the case of a multiple pregnancy Other risk factors: • invasive group B streptococcal infection in a previous baby or maternal group B streptococcal colonisation, bacteriuria or infection in the current pregnancy • pre-term birth following spontaneous labour before 37 weeks' gestation • confirmed rupture of membranes for more than 18 hours before a pre-term birth • confirmed rupture of membranes for more than 24 hours before a term birth [2026] • suspected or confirmed maternal sepsis in the intrapartum or early postpartum period [2021, amended 2026] • suspected or confirmed chorioamnionitis [2021, amended 2026]

Consider establishing hospital systems to provide blood culture results 36 hours after starting antibiotics for early-onset neonatal infection, to allow timely stopping of treatment and discharge from hospital. [2012]
